title: Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl
description: Following its prize-winning premiere at the Venice Film Festival and a whirlwind tour of the fall festival circuit, “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapt
body:
Following its prize-winning premiere at the Venice Film Festival and a whirlwind tour of the fall festival circuit, “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” by Greek filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou, celebrates its homecoming this week at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, where it’s competing for top honors in the festival’s main international competition.

	Inspired by true events, Lentzou’s sophomore feature follows the unruly, melancholic 15-year-old Jo — played by arresting newcomer Evia Andriopoulou — as she navigates the ups and downs of a typical day in a typical teenager’s life. Drifting through a series of seemingly unrelated and inconsequential events, an otherwise ordinary day is turned upside-down with the arrival of Phaedra (Anastasia Gouliamou), a bookish classmate whose warbling rendition of an old love ballad reduces Jo to tears. In an instant, her life — her drab, unremarkable day — becomes full of possibility, hurtling toward both tragedy and transformation.
	

	“A Day in the Life of Jo” premiered in the Venice Film Festival’s Horizons strand, where it won the award for best director. It’s since gone on to a healthy festival run, including stops at the New York Film Festival, the BFI London Film Festival and the Busan Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in North America.

	Speaking to Variety in Thessaloniki, Lentzou explains that the film was inspired by tragic real-life events: the 2008 killing of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose murder at the hands of Athens police sparked nationwide protests and riots — an event that marked a brutal coming of age for Lentzou’s generation and is still commemorated with massive protests every year.
	

	While “this tragic incident served as the spark for the film,” the director says, it’s ultimately little more than a stepping stone for a profound and often moving meditation on life and the mystery of what comes after. Progressing in a loose, episodic fashion — “all days, at least my days, feel fragmented and non-linear,” Lentzou notes — it’s organized around a series of mundane events, all of which lead to an explosive, audacious and formally bold conclusion.

	There are squabbles with Jo’s mother (Eleni Vergeti), the girl’s sole guardian since her parents’ divorce, and a visit from her dad. Other, enigmatic encounters recall the signs and symbols that came to Jo in a dream, hinting at the porous borders between sleeping and waking, between conscious and unconscious — or, Lentzou suggests, between life and whatever comes next. At its heart is what the director describes as “the film’s existential game of who and what we truly are.”

	The movie is carried by a startling performance from debutante Andriopoulou, who Lentzou says she discovered “after an exhausting and admittedly disappointing two-month casting session” that ultimately led to an open call.

	“My hopes were not very high, yet at some point Evita enters, shyly and very, very gently, and it felt like meeting a part of me,” Lentzou explains. “I sensed a wound, a small breakage despite the youth of her age, and this is what led me to choosing her: a girl with whom I could communicate deeply.”

	The director went on to praise Andriopoulou’s performance as being “full of pure, honest emotion,” insisting that a recent acting prize at the Euro Balkan Film Festival in Rome would be “the start of a series of accolades” for the film’s young star.

	Lentzou also credits DoP Grimm Vandekerckhove for his striking cinematography, which captures the complicated play of emotions across Andriopoulou’s richly expressive face and imbues even quotidian objects and gestures with poetry and meaning.

	“The key in the visual approach, the big question hovering over our heads, was how to depict the invisible (already a contrast in terms), how to make the subtle presence of another awareness felt through our camera work,” Lentzou says. “I cannot stress enough how much of the film’s insane success is owed to Grimm’s contribution and faith in the project.”
	

	“A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” is produced by Avion Films and Atalante Productions in co-production with Kelek Film, 4A4 Productions, ERT and Haris & Co. Lucky Number is handling world sales.

	The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

schema.headline: Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl

title: AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage
description: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately f
body:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the next several days, the stoppage left many Hollywood insiders grounded on one of the busiest travel weekends of the year. 

	AFM was hit hard by the standstill, and several events were canceled as dealmakers were preparing for their final days at the major sales function. Ryan Werner, president of global cinema at Neon, told Variety he was unsure if he could make it to AFM on Saturday for the studio’s party. He mentioned “our flights” when referring to travel plans, likely meaning several members of the Neon team were shut down on the way to Los Angeles. 
	

	One agency source told Variety that when the FAA shut down travel, their department broke out in a panic to see if anyone could still make their scheduled appearances at Saturday’s Governors Awards, which take place at the Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood. 

	“Once the news happened, everyone jumped on the phone to see if anyone is going to be able to make it to L.A. for the Governors Awards,” they said. “One agent has a client traveling through Europe with no idea how he will get back for his next things in the U.S., so they might have to hang out in Canada to at least be close.”

	TMZ reported that “Baywatch” star Brooks Nader’s private jet was stopped in New York just before taking off for Louisiana. The outlet also shared a video of “Bachelorette” star Kaitlyn Bristowe stuck in an airport. Flava Flav and Morgan Fairchild both took to social media to share that their travel plans were affected. Variety also confirmed that the Sharpe Family Singers and actor Isaac Robinson Smith were all left stuck at the airport. 
	

	News of the flight stoppage broke around 1 p.m. PT. At the time, the FAA said the pause was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin later appeared on Fox News and clarified that it was a “telecommunications outage” that caused the backup and that there was no indication of a “nefarious attack” against the United States. 

	The FAA announced around 6 p.m. PT that the nationwide ground stoppage was canceled.

schema.headline: AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage

title: Kamal Khera Named New Canadian Consul General In Los Angeles, Will Meet With Studios
description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed a new Consul General in Los Angeles, who says she hopes to inspire a renewed sense of unity betwe
body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed a new Consul General in Los Angeles, who says she hopes to inspire a renewed sense of unity between Canada and the U.S.

	The Honourable Kamal Khera was introduced as Canada’s Consul General in Los Angeles on Thursday night at a reception at Canada House, the Consul General’s residence in the city’s Hancock Park neighborhood. A longtime Member of Parliament in Canada, Khera held multiple roles in the federal Cabinet under Carney, and predecessor Justin Trudeau, including serving as the Minister of Health, Minister of Seniors, and Minister of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities. The 37-year-old Brampton, Ontario native now heads across the border, where she will be representing Canada across Southern California, Arizona and Nevada.
	

	In prepared remarks Thursday, Khera said her first order of business will be to address the growing distrust between Canadians in her region and the U.S., a divide which has been spurred by President Trump’s ongoing trade war, along with comments he made last year about Canada becoming the “51st state.” With almost 50,000 Canadians living in Southern California, and thousands more across Arizona and Nevada, the three states represent the largest contingent of Canadians in the U.S. (in the 80s, Los Angeles was said to have had the fourth-largest Canadian population of any city in North America).

	Khera stressed that there is a history and bond between the two countries that should not be forgotten. “Canada and the United States share a partnership that runs deep, built over generations through shared interests, common security, economic ties, and friendships between our people,” Khera remarked. “The United States has been, and will remain, our closest friend, ally, and partner,” she continued, acknowledging that “we are living through a period of considerable change. But one thing my years in public life have taught me is that relationships are not defined by a single moment,” she said. “They are built over time, through trust, mutual respect, and a shared commitment to working together. And that is the spirit I hope to bring to my time here.”
	



	

									John Sciulli
	



	Khera will likely be pressed to address the so-called Hollywood Exodus, which has seen a number of film and television productions move north of the border (Canada currently offers a 16% labor credit on top of a 30% incentive in the province of Manitoba). Of course, Canada has also seen its share of success with homegrown exports like the surprise Bell Media hit, “Heated Rivalry,” which was later acquired by HBO Max.

	While Khera joked that friends have already been texting her for “Hollywood gossip,” the Consul General is expected to sit down with various interest groups and studios in the coming months. Still, she was quick to note that California, Arizona and Nevada have long been places to foster collaboration, not only in arts and entertainment, but in technology and industry as well. “Whether it’s connecting Canadian businesses with American investors, advancing collaboration in aerospace and defense, supporting our creative industries, or bringing together innovators and researchers, there is tremendous potential in what we can accomplish together,” she said. “And I want our Consulate to be an active partner in turning those opportunities into lasting relationships and meaningful results.”

	Prior to her diplomatic appointment, Khera served nearly a decade in the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa. First elected in 2015 at the age of 26, she was one of the youngest women ever elected to the House of Commons. Before entering public life, Khera worked as a registered nurse in oncology. 

	Khera replaces outgoing Consul General Zaib Shaikh, who departed last November.

schema.headline: Kamal Khera Named New Canadian Consul General In Los Angeles, Will Meet With Studios

title: Amid Flight Stop, Ari Emanuel Slams Pete Buttigieg for Making ‘Zero Progress’ Modernizing FAA: ‘You Left a Failing System in Place’
description: As the nation’s air traffic ground to a halt Friday afternoon amid an FAA ground stop, Ari Emanuel had strong words for former transportation secre
body:
As the nation’s air traffic ground to a halt Friday afternoon amid an FAA ground stop, Ari Emanuel had strong words for former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg. 

	The WME executive chairman posted on X, “No one’s hands are clean here. However, Mr. Secretary Buttigieg, you had four years in the job and infrastructure money, yet made zero progress modernizing the FAA. You left a failing system in place. THANKS!”


No one’s hands are clean here. However, Mr. Secretary Buttigieg, you had four years in the job and infrastructure money, yet made zero progress modernizing the FAA. You left a failing system in place. THANKS!— Ari Emanuel (@AriEmanuel) November 13, 2026


	Buttigieg left his post at the end of the Biden administration. Current transportation secretary Sean Duffy addressed the public just after the flight stop was lifted on Friday evening, referencing his demands to Congress for modernization funds. “I can’t build things if I don’t have money,” Duffy said. “We should talk to our senators and members of Congress to say, ‘We don’t deserve this.’”
	

	Duffy said making upgrades was necessary but admitted it may have introduced instability into the air control system. “By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said, adding, “I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”

	Emanuel’s tweet was quickly answered by more than 3,000 commenters questioning why he was blaming a previous administration. “Yeah let’s blame the guys from 2+ years ago when the FAA has been a burning dumpster fire since Duffy stepped into office,” said one commenter.

	Others commented, “Did someone hack your account? Two years into a new administration and no specific evidence yet as to what failed. And your first go-to is blaming Buttigieg?”
	

	Another commenter referenced Ari Emanuel’s brother Rahm Emanuel, who is seen to be angling for a 2023 presidential bid. “I know your goal here is to attack one of your brother’s presidential rivals, but I am certain it will backfire in the eyes of dem primary voters,” the commenter said. 

	Meanwhile, Buttigieg was stranded at Denver airport, and after watching the press conference from Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, Buttigieg told the New York Times, “You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” Buttigieg said. “I have questions.”

schema.headline: Amid Flight Stop, Ari Emanuel Slams Pete Buttigieg for Making ‘Zero Progress’ Modernizing FAA: ‘You Left a Failing System in Place’

title: ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story
description: Why did the chicken cross the road? In “Hen,” the answer is, as ever, to get to the other side. But the stakes are a little higher and more urgent
body:
Why did the chicken cross the road? In “Hen,” the answer is, as ever, to get to the other side. But the stakes are a little higher and more urgent than that in György Pálfi unassuming marvel of a creature feature: When its gallinaceous protagonist is forced across a busy highway, it’s because a hungry fox is very much on her tailfeathers. That hunter and prey in this scenario are both played by real live animals is a large part what makes “Hen” riveting: Made without CGI, with a predominantly non-human ensemble that includes eight fowl playing the lead role alone, it’s a sustained cinematic feat of fauna-wrangling unlike any other. But it’s not the miraculous novelty of the production that crosses your mind as you’re watching: In the moment, your heart pounds for that poor, dumb but surprisingly resourceful chicken, and you lock completely into her simultaneously small and vast survival saga. 
	

	Coming from most filmmakers, “Hen” — which premiered in Toronto’s Platform competition last year, earning an honorable mention from the jury — would count as an eccentric project. But from Hungarian auteur Pálfi, whose consistently experimental oeuvre includes 2006’s Cannes-selected, shape-shifting body horror “Taxidermia” and 2018’s labyrinthine mixed-media Stanislaw Lem adaptation “His Master’s Voice,” this may be the most narratively conventional film he’s ever assembled: a grandly linear hero’s journey in which the hero just happens to be a resplendently scarlet-combed and treacle-plumed chicken, whose antagonists along the way run the gamut from wild predators to human traffickers. No life form is given precedence over another, as “Hen” limns a tense dog-eat-dog-eat-bird ecosystem — the world we all know and struggle through, just from a different vantage point.
	

	The hen in question remains nameless and voiceless from beginning to end — though the birds playing her all get star billing by name in the closing credits. (Eszti, Szandi, Feri, Enci, Eti, Enikő, Nóra and Anett, to give them their due.) Pálfi has little interest in directly anthropomorphic storytelling, and while his film is a rather eventfully scripted fiction, it aims for documentary-style naturalism and spontaneity. The obvious recent comparison point is Jerzy Skolimowski’s Oscar-nominated donkey odyssey “EO,” minus that film’s more expressionistic flourishes; Robert Bresson’s “Au Hasard Balthasar,” too, minus at least some of its despairing tragedy.

	It begins in a cramped industrial farm somewhere in rural Greece, where the hen’s life begins with a startlingly graphic egg-laying scene. (If you’ve ever wondered what a chicken’s cloaca looks like up close, Pálfi has you covered.) After the fledgling chick cracks her way into the outside world — standing out from the vast crowd with her uniformly dark plumage — she soon learns the cruel ways of commercial poultry-rearing and, in time, seeks a different destiny. A heart-in-mouth chain of circumstances enables her escape; via a serious of perilous scrapes, she eventually winds up at a coastal smallholding, owned by a family who get by running a shabby café on the premises, alongside other, less legal activities.

	There, she finds herself trapped again in the owners’ chicken coop, and put to work laying eggs: a less grim fate than the one that awaited her in the farm where she was born, perhaps, but an unhappy one just the same. Though Pálfi lightens matters with some droll music cues — the coop’s resident rooster is introduced to the grandiose strains of a romantic ballad by Greek favorite Grigoris Mpithikotsis — the film doesn’t shy from the traumatizing impact of what effectively amounts, for our feathered heroine, to recurring sexual assault, and the repeated theft of her eggs. 

	And so she escapes, thrillingly, and more than once — motivated, it seems, by little more than some unknowing, unspoken sense that there has to be something else out there for her. In a particularly dark stab of irony, a key chance at liberation comes via her owners’ reckless venture into the trafficking of refugees. Though “Hen” maintains a sly comic sensibility throughout, there’s solemn substance to how it shows the interconnected abuse of human and animal rights alike, adding up to a portrait of a world sliding off its moral axis. 
	

	That deft command and calibration of tone is as remarkable as the film’s seamless technical fluency, with every below-the-line contribution vital in cleaving to the chicken’s perspective. Vividly detailed sound design keeps us in her tiny headspace; ditto Giorgos Karvelas’ lithe, nimble cinematography, fully alert to her rhythm of movement and occasional, unpredictable moments of flighty rebellion. Editor Lehmhényi Réka, meanwhile, achieves the extraordinary feat of forging one coherent and characterful performance from footage of multiple birds — a patchworked star turn that invites and earns our complete emotional investment. A madly impractical and richly felt vision that pretty much required Pálfi to put all his eggs in one basket, “Hen” is a risk that pays off in heartening style.

schema.headline: ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story

title: Michael Mann Seeks to Reclaim Rights to Original ‘Heat’ Screenplay
description: Michael Mann, who is set to begin shooting the long-awaited “Heat 2” in January, is in a legal dispute with New Regency as he seeks to reclaim the
body:
Michael Mann, who is set to begin shooting the long-awaited “Heat 2” in January, is in a legal dispute with New Regency as he seeks to reclaim the copyright to his screenplay for the original film.

	New Regency produced “Heat,” released in 1995. The company filed a lawsuit on Friday arguing that it still owns the copyright to the original screenplay.

	Earlier this year, Mann’s lawyers sent termination notices invoking the right to reclaim the copyright. New Regency argues that the screenplay was a “work made for hire,” and is thus ineligible for copyright termination.
	

	New Regency argues that Mann’s termination action clouds its ownership of the original “Heat,” and is seeking a declaration that the termination notices are void.

	Mann’s lawyers intend to fight the lawsuit “vigorously,” his reps said in a statement.

	“We will vigorously defend this action and are confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann’s statutory rights under the Copyright Act,” a spokesperson said. “This filing has to do with original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s and which evolved into the iconic 1995 film ‘Heat’ that Mann wrote, produced and directed. After 40 years Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”

	Mann developed the characters and the story that would become “Heat” over two decades, beginning in the 1970s. According to the lawsuit, Warner Bros. acquired the rights to the “Heat” screenplay in 1994 in a deal with Mann’s loan-out company. The suit alleges that deal was explicitly a “work made for hire” agreement — not an assignment of rights — and that therefore it cannot be terminated.
	

	Authors are allowed to terminate assignments of rights after 35 years under the Copyright Act.

	According to the suit, Mann’s lawyers initially told New Regency that Mann had assigned his rights to his loan-out companies in 1988, and was thus seeking to terminate that agreement. New Regency sought a copy of that agreement, and was told it was an oral agreement, the suit states.

	“The Oral Assignment on which the First Termination Notice is based supposedly derives from an oral agreement that Mann allegedly made with himself, in which Mann, like a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts, simultaneously spoke on his own individual behalf, as well as on behalf of MMCo. and ZZY,” the lawsuit states.

	Two subsequent termination notices were submitted cited other agreements, both of which New Regency claims are also invalid.

	Warner Bros. was originally set to produce “Heat 2,” but backed out of the project last year. Amazon MGM Studios has since acquired the film. Both Mann and New Regency have done deals with Amazon that account for the copyright dispute, with Mann assigning any rights he may reclaim to Amazon, according to the complaint.

	In other words, however the dispute comes out, “Heat 2” should be unaffected.

	“For clarification, this is unrelated to production of Heat 2 which will begin shooting on January 19,” Mann’s rep said in a statement.

schema.headline: Michael Mann Seeks to Reclaim Rights to Original ‘Heat’ Screenplay

title: European Film Award Nominations: ‘Fatherland’ Reigns Over Contest, Followed by ‘La Bola Negra’
description:
Nov 14, 2026 2:28am PT	
	

	
		European Film Award Nominations: ‘Fatherland’ Reigns Over Contest, Followed by ‘La Bola Negra’
body:
Nov 14, 2026 2:28am PT	
	

	
		European Film Award Nominations: ‘Fatherland’ Reigns Over Contest, Followed by ‘La Bola Negra’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Agata Grzybowska
	

		
	
				

	Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” which centers on the relationship between the writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika, leads the contest for the 39th European Film Awards, followed close behind by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s “La Bola Negra.”

	“Fatherland” has 11 EFA nominations, while “La Bola Negra,” a time-spanning epic based on a work of Federico Garcia Lorca, took 10 nominations. Both films shared the best director prize at Cannes.
	

	The nominations, which were announced by the European Film Academy on Saturday at the Thessaloniki Film Festival in Greece, were based on the votes of the 5,700 members of the academy. The winners will be unveiled on Jan. 16 in Athens.

	In third place was Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” with five nominations, followed by Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose” with four nominations.

	Pawlikowski, Calvo and Ambrossi, and Mungiu are competing for best director, alongside Sandra Wollner for “Everytime” and Andrey Zvyagintsev for “Minotaur,” winner of Cannes’ Grand Prix.

	Sandra Hüller is nominated for both “Fatherland” and “Rose” in the best actress category, where she competes with Penélope Cruz for “Bunker,” Léa Seydoux for “Gentle Monster,” Renate Reinsve for “Fjord” and Mathilde Arcel for “Woman Unknown,” the winner for best actress in Venice.

	Nominations for best actor went to Javier Bardem for “The Beloved,” Andrew Scott for “Elsinore,” Sebastian Stan for “Fjord,” Swann Arlaud for “A Man of His Time” and Hanns Zischler for “Fatherland.”
	

	May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown,” the winner of Venice’s Golden Lion, had three nominations.

	Two nominations each were taken by “Bunker,” “Coward,” “Elsinore,” “Everytime” and “Minotaur.”

	The nominations for best documentary were for “NAZA,” winner of the Special Jury Prize in Venice, “Letters From the Silenced Country,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” which was the winner for best documentary in Cannes, “To Hold a Mountain” and “Whispers in the Woods.”

	The animated films that were nominated were “Viva Carmen,” “Lucy Lost,” “Jim Queen,” “Iron Boy” and “In Waves.”

title: Spain’s FICX Gijón Festival Bets Big on International, Regional and Local Talent
description: GIJÓN, Spain — Taking place in northern Spain under two monhs after the San Sebastián International Film Festival and linked to it by the Cross Roa
body:
GIJÓN, Spain — Taking place in northern Spain under two monhs after the San Sebastián International Film Festival and linked to it by the Cross Roads initiative, the 64th Gijón International Film Festival (FICX)  lineup stacks many of the year’s most talked-about features from international festivals such as Cannes, Berlin, Venice and Sundance. 

	At the same time, running Nov. 13-20, the festival serves as a springboard for new local talent into the international arena, which the festival has championed for decades.
	

	FICX’s influence extends to the new Spanish talent currently rising with recognition: Oliver Laxe (“Sirât”), Jonás Trueba (“The Other Way Around”) and Carla Simon (“Alcarràs”) are closely linked with Gijón. Both Laxe and Trueba showcased their first works at the festival and have built long careers since their early FICX selections. Simón had her very own first retrospective at Gijón.

	The Gijón Festival has a long standing tradition of mixing rising and established talent, top-tier international and regional voice rubbing shoulders, becoming a beacon for emerging talent. 

	This year’s edition opened Nov. 13 with James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” screening in Gijón’s main Albar section. Gray’s previous feature, “Armageddon Time,” also opened the 2022 Gijón festival.

	Closing the festival on Nov. 20 is Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” described by Variety’s Owen Gleiberman as “a cleverly crafted crowd-pleaser, all designed to tap into the love of ‘Rocky’ that has never gone away.”

	“On one side we bring big names from the international industry, as we’ve done in previous editions,” explained FICX director Alejandro Díaz Castaño. “We also bring top-Spanish talent and well-established filmmakers  such as Albert Serra (“Sixteen Moments of My Life”) or Hal Hartley (“Where To Land”).
	

	Albar, the festival’s main competition, includes 21 features aiming for the top prize. Albar’s selection includes Cannes Directors’ Fortnight winner Clio Barnard’s “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,” Grant Lee’s Berlin Silver Bear winner “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” and Visar Morina’s “Shame and Money,” winner of the World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury prize at Sundance.

	“I think we ended up having many unclassifiable features, which do not fully fit into more structured selections because of their strong auteurist component,” explained Díaz Castaño. “Here at Gijón, we are really into that mix of genres, those hybrids that tend to live on the margins.”

	Among the Albar titles is Valeska Grisebach’s Cannes Jury Prize winner “The Dreamed Adventure.” No stranger to either the city or the festival, Grisebach’s previous work “Longing” took the festival’s best feature prize back in 2006.

	Hong Sang-soo, a Gijón favorite who has won FICX best feature prize three times, arrives at this edition’s Albar with “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” which scooped the best director prize at Locarno.

	Radu Jude, another Gijón’s regular who scored Albar’s top prize in 2023 with “Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World,” returns with “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” which premiered at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight.

	“We are also lucky to have some regular, highly talented attendees from both the local and international landscape, such as Lisandro Alonso (“Eureka”), Albert Serra, Radu Jude and Hong Sangsoo,” added Díaz Castaño.

	László Nemes’ “Moulin,” Jeanne Herry’s “Garance” and Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries” round out a competition that includes Mads Mengel’s Karlovy Vary winner “The Guest.”

	Nicolas Pariser’s Venice contender “One Minute to Midnight” will screen out of competition. “The Italian coda is sweet, allowing Pariser to redeem the concept of love from the cynicism of a world wary of romance,” wrote Variety’s Jay Weissberg.

	Retueyos, focusing on directors promoting their second or third feature, opens with Pierre Le Gall’s “Flesh and Fuel,” winner of Cannes’ Queer Palme Révélation prize. It also includes Venice Orizzonti winner Ann Sirot and Raphaël Balboni’s “Un détour par Diane.”
	

	The festival’s Premiere section brings international features to Spain for their premieres. It has expanded to 16 titles. Among attending filmmakers is Gregg Araki, who returns to the festival with Sundance title “I Want Your Sex,” starring Cooper Hoffman and Olivia Wilde. Araki first visited Gijón in 1996, presenting three of his early works, “The Living End,” “Totally F***ed Up” and “The Doom Generation.” He was also the subject of a 1999 FICX retrospective.

	Other Spain premieres take in Céline Sciamma’s cinematic essay “Tutti Frutti”; Jia Zhangke’s Cannes title “Torino Shadow”; Cédric Kahn’s Venice screener “A Place to Heal”; Ulrike Ottinger’s vampire fantasy “The Blood Countess,” starring Isabelle Huppert; and Mohammad Rasoulof’s 39-minute “Sense of Water.”

	Sangsoo will also be on hand for Gijón presentation of “The Day She Returns,” which is set to open in U.S. theaters next month.

	Thanks to the festival’s relation with its audience, its success on ticket sales and its relentless pursuit of partners and collaborations, five San Sebastián Festival titles arrive at Gijón as part of the festival’s Cross Roads initiative. The list includes Fred Cavayé’s “Les Mirsérables,” Jesse Steinberg’s “The Debut” and Javier Ruiz Caldera’s “5 More Minutes.”

	Gijón continues to support talent, collaborating with the Asturias Paraiso Natural Film Commision on FICX Pro, its industry wing and on the Semilleru project development lab, which provide opportunities for local  Asturian and Spanish professionals. 

	“What we aim to do is to bring the city together and push together and rally support behind the festival, working hard with local and regional entities, local government, and private initiatives and citizens. The festival becomes like a hub where everyone tunes in to connect and where everyone can find their place,” added Diaz Castaño.

title: Jason Voorhees Makes His Animated Debut in New ‘Never Hike Alone’ Short
description: More than 46 years after his big-screen debut in the slasher classic “Friday the 13th,” hulking horror icon Jason Voorhees is about to prove that h
body:
More than 46 years after his big-screen debut in the slasher classic “Friday the 13th,” hulking horror icon Jason Voorhees is about to prove that his machete cuts just as deep in animation. The hockey-masked killer returns in “Never Hike Alone: Ghosts in the Fog,” a new 10-minute animated film from independent production company Womp Stomp Films.



	Premiering Friday, Nov. 13, at 5 p.m. PT, and streaming for free on the Womp Stomp Films YouTube channel, the story follows an unlucky trio of friends whose relaxing weekend camping trip takes a gory turn when they become lost in the fog surrounding the infamous Camp Crystal Lake.
	

	Founded in 2016 by filmmaker Vincente DiSanti, Womp Stomp Films has built a devoted following with its ambitious series of “Friday the 13th” fan films. The saga began with DiSanti’s 2017 short “Never Hike Alone,” followed by the winter-set prequel “Never Hike in the Snow” in 2020. The feature-length sequel “Never Hike Alone 2” arrived in 2023, featuring “Friday the 13th Part VI: Jason Lives” actors Thom Mathews and Vincent Guastaferro reprising their original roles as Tommy Jarvis and Sheriff Rick Cologne.

	The “Never Hike Alone” films have relied on crowdfunding campaigns to help finance their increasingly elaborate productions. The fan-supported approach has allowed DiSanti and his collaborators to expand the saga while making the finished films available to watch for free online.

	Although the “Never Hike Alone” films feature copyrighted characters, settings and storylines from the official “Friday the 13th” franchise, Womp Stomp Films operates independently of the studios that own the Jason Voorhees property. The company follows a set of self-imposed guidelines designed to avoid copyright disputes, including making its films available for free, using crowdfunding exclusively for production expenses and not turning a profit. Each film includes an on-screen disclaimer acknowledging that the rights holders can challenge the production. So far, the franchise owners have not taken action to stop the films.
	

	“Ghosts in the Fog” marks the fourth installment in the Womp Stomp series and its first venture into animation. The short arrives amid a resurgence of activity surrounding the “Friday the 13th” franchise. Peacock debuted its A24-produced prequel series “Crystal Lake,” starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, in October. Meanwhile, it was announced Friday that Steve Miner, who directed 1981’s “Friday the 13th Part 2” and 1982’s “Friday the 13th Part III,” will return to helm the franchise’s 13th feature film, scheduled for theatrical release in 2027. The new movie will mark Jason’s first big-screen appearance since the 2009 reboot.

	“Ghosts in the Fog” was produced in collaboration with Mako Animation Studio, a Mexico-based company specializing in 2D animation. Founded in 2015 by Juan Rivera, who co-directed the new short alongside DiSanti, the studio’s previous projects include the animated YouTube series “John Death.”

            Presley Gerber’s Hollywood Hills home is hitting the market less than two months after his tragic death … and the property comes with a multimillion dollar price tag … TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The late model’s Los Angeles pad listed Friday for $3.595 million, according to real estate records obtained by TMZ.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The 3,000 square foot mid-century home features 4 bedrooms and 3 bathrooms … along with a heated pool, Jacuzzi, cold plunge, sauna and a separate guest house.
      

            And there’s plenty of privacy … the gated property is surrounded by lush greenery and canyon views, with sprawling indoor-outdoor living spaces.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported … famous parents, Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber were seen leaving the Hollywood Hills property the day after Presley died. Rande was also photographed returning to the home days later.
      
    
            We broke the story ... Presley died September 20 at a Santa Monica rehab facility.
      
    
            Authorities investigated his death as a suspected overdose, though his official cause of death had not been determined.
      
    
            The home previously sold for $3.4 million in March 2023.

title: DJ Khaled Shows Off Dramatic Weight Loss After Hitting 300 Pounds
body:
DJ Khaled

            DJ Khaled is dropping more than just hit records these days ... the music mogul has shed nearly 100 pounds, and he's giving Wegovy some of the credit for his jaw-dropping transformation!
      
    
            The "All I Do Is Win" singer revealed to PEOPLE he was pushing 300 pounds before getting serious about his health ... and it took a frightening moment onstage to realize something needed to change.
      
    
            Khaled says he was performing in October 2025 when he dropped to his knees to give thanks ... but struggled to get back up. To make matters worse, several friends noticed he was breathing heavily and expressed concern about his health.
      

            The 50-year-old says he was already working out and trying to eat better, but needed some extra help ... so he turned to the weight-loss drug Wegovy after consulting his doctor.
      
    
            Khaled says he's now weighing in between 200 and 212 pounds, down from roughly 295 to 300. He credits the medication with helping him shed 75 pounds over the past year.
      
    
            But Khaled isn't just letting the injections do the heavy lifting ... he's also hitting the golf course up to six times a week, walking all 18 holes instead of cruising around in a cart and racking up more than 10K steps a day.
      
    
            The Grammy winner says he's feeling healthier and has more energy ... and he's now hoping to get down to 200 pounds.
      
    
            All he does is win ... and apparently lose, too!!!
